# Sequencing Measures Shares of a Finite Library

RNA-seq samples molecules from a library with finite sequencing capacity. Let
$a_{gj}>0$ denote the amount of sequenceable material from gene $g$ in sample
$j$, after feature-specific capture effects are included, and let

$$
A_j=\sum_{h=1}^{G}a_{hj}.
$$

Conditional on a total of $N_j$ assigned fragments, a simple multinomial view is

$$
(K_{1j},\ldots,K_{Gj})\mid N_j
\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}
\left(N_j;p_{1j},\ldots,p_{Gj}\right),
\qquad
p_{gj}=\frac{a_{gj}}{A_j}.
$$

Only the proportions $p_{gj}$ are observed through counts. Multiplying every
$a_{gj}$ in one sample by the same constant leaves every $p_{gj}$ unchanged.
Total RNA abundance is therefore not identifiable from ordinary relative counts
alone. A normalization factor supplies a reference-scale assumption or imports
external information; it cannot recover an absolute scale from no information.

# The Mechanism of Composition Bias

For the same gene in samples 1 and 2,

$$
\frac{p_{g2}}{p_{g1}}
=\frac{a_{g2}}{a_{g1}}\frac{A_1}{A_2}.
$$

The observed relative fold change combines the gene's abundance change with a
sample-wide composition term. If one abundant transcript increases enough to
raise $A_2$, an unchanged gene with $a_{g2}=a_{g1}$ has
$p_{g2}/p_{g1}=A_1/A_2<1$. It appears down-regulated even though its absolute
amount did not change.

This denominator coupling explains several empirical patterns:

- a few highly expressed genes can shift the apparent center of log fold changes;
- total-count or counts-per-million scaling can propagate those changes to every
  other gene;
- more reads narrow counting uncertainty around the biased relative contrast;
- a normalization method can change estimated fold changes without changing raw
  counts because it changes the effective sample scale.

Composition bias is not synonymous with biological error. A genuine global
transcriptional response changes composition. The problem is interpretive: a
relative assay cannot distinguish a global abundance shift from a technical
change in sampled material unless the design supplies a reference.

# Normalization Factors as Model Offsets

A gene-wise negative binomial model can write

$$
K_{gj}\sim\operatorname{NB}(\mu_{gj},\alpha_g),
\qquad
\log(\mu_{gj})=log(N_jf_j)+\mathbf x_j^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta_g,
$$

where $f_j$ is a composition normalization factor and $N_jf_j$ is an effective
library size. Some software instead combines depth and composition into one size
factor $s_j$:

$$
\log(\mu_{gj})=\log(s_j)+\mathbf x_j^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta_g.
$$

The factors are relative and require a constraint, commonly
$\prod_jf_j=1$ or a geometric mean of one. A factor below one in edgeR reduces
the effective library size and is algebraically equivalent to scaling that
sample's counts upward for descriptive comparison. The fitted count model keeps
raw counts as responses and uses the effective size as an offset.

# How Robust Scaling Methods Define the Reference

## TMM

For sample $j$ and reference $r$, TMM begins with

$$
M_g=\log_2\left(\frac{K_{gj}/N_j}{K_{gr}/N_r}\right),
\qquad
A_g=\frac{1}{2}\log_2
\left(\frac{K_{gj}}{N_j}\frac{K_{gr}}{N_r}\right).
$$

After excluding zero counts and trimming genes with extreme $M_g$ or $A_g$, it
computes a precision-weighted mean

$$
\bar M_{jr}^{\mathrm{trim}}
=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal T}w_gM_g}
{\sum_{g\in\mathcal T}w_g},
\qquad
f_{j:r}=2^{\bar M_{jr}^{\mathrm{trim}}}.
$$

The trimming set $\mathcal T$ prevents strongly changing or extremely abundant
features from defining the reference, while $w_g$ downweights noisy log ratios.
Rescaling factors across libraries imposes the identifying constraint.

## Median-of-ratios

The DESeq family compares each gene with its across-sample geometric-mean
pseudo-reference and takes the median ratio within a sample:

$$
\hat s_j=\operatorname{median}_{g:G_g>0}
\left(\frac{K_{gj}}{G_g}\right),
\qquad
G_g=\left(\prod_vK_{gv}\right)^{1/m}.
$$

On the log scale, this centers the median gene-wise sample-to-reference change at
zero. TMM uses trimming and approximate precision weights; median-of-ratios uses
a median. Both rely on a sufficiently large informative set whose true changes
are absent or reasonably balanced. Neither can identify the correct absolute
scale when nearly all genes change in the same direction.

# The Assumption Must Match the Biology

The usual robust scaling assumption is often paraphrased as “most genes are not
differentially expressed.” The operational requirement is more nuanced: after
excluding influential features, the reference genes' changes must locate a
stable center. Many genes may change if upward and downward changes are balanced;
a smaller asymmetric set may still cause failure if it dominates counts or the
chosen center.

Examples that challenge this assumption include:

- transcription-factor perturbations producing broad directional shifts;
- RNA degradation or depletion affecting large transcript classes;
- very different tissues or cell-type mixtures;
- small RNA experiments dominated by a few species;
- targeted panels with few candidate reference features; and
- conditions that change total RNA per cell.

Removing ribosomal, mitochondrial, or other dominant features may stabilize the
factor when those features are technical contaminants. It may instead discard a
real biological change. The exclusion rule should follow the measurement target
and be reported, not selected merely to make fold changes look centered.

# External and Feature-specific Scale Information

When the stable-majority assumption is implausible, scale can come from a
prespecified control set or external spike-ins. If spike-in molecules are added
in a known amount per cell, per unit input, or per sample, that choice defines
which absolute quantity is calibrated. Spike-ins are useful only if addition,
recovery, and capture are reliable and if their denominator matches the desired
estimand.

A single factor cannot correct sample-specific gene biases. GC-content, gene
length, mappability, or transcript-level abundance estimation may require
gene-by-sample normalization factors $NF_{gj}$:

$$
\mu_{gj}=NF_{gj}q_{gj}.
$$

Those factors address a different problem from one composition multiplier per
sample. Likewise, batch covariates, latent-factor adjustment, and cell-type
composition models are not substitutes for exposure normalization.

# Experimental Design and Replication

For a condition contrast, independently sampled donors, organisms, or cultures
are experimental units. Reads, genes, technical lanes, and aliquots are not
replicates for that contrast. Genes provide repeated evidence for estimating a
nuisance normalization factor, but their shared sample means that they cannot
replace between-unit replication.

Distribute conditions across extraction, library-preparation, and sequencing
batches. Include controls across batches when cross-run scaling matters. If
condition and batch are completely confounded, normalization cannot decide
whether a global shift is biological or technical. Randomization and bridge
samples create information that no downstream scaling formula can reconstruct.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis

No diagnostic proves the normalization assumption from relative counts alone,
because the missing absolute scale is an identification problem. Diagnostics can
nevertheless expose instability and implausible consequences.

| Question | Diagnostic | Sensitivity analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Do a few genes dominate the libraries? | Cumulative count shares and top-feature fractions | Re-estimate factors with prespecified dominant classes excluded |
| Is the log-ratio center stable? | M-value or relative log-expression plots by condition | Compare TMM, median-of-ratios, and justified control-based factors |
| Are factors driven by low counts? | Plot gene-wise ratios against average abundance | Filter uninformative features before factor estimation using a documented rule |
| Do known controls remain stable? | Control log ratios and residuals | Use independent control sets or spike-in calibration when valid |
| Is a sample anomalous beyond scale? | Replicate distances and residual patterns after normalization | Investigate quality; do not force a failed sample onto the reference |
| Are conclusions normalization-dependent? | Compare log fold changes, standard errors, rankings, and FDR decisions | Report instability and narrow the claim rather than choosing the preferred result |

The analysis record should include raw library sizes, estimated factors,
features used to estimate them, method and software version, handling of zeros,
and sensitivity results for important contrasts.

# Statistical versus Biological Interpretation

Suppose a stimulus doubles the total RNA per cell while each gene preserves its
share of the transcriptome. Ordinary relative RNA-seq counts show no gene-wise
change. Statistically, the data support stable proportions under the chosen
scale. Biologically, transcripts per cell doubled. Without cell counts, calibrated
spike-ins, or another external denominator, both states produce the same relative
composition.

Conversely, after robust normalization a gene may show a two-fold relative
increase with a precise interval across donors. That is a population estimate
relative to the normalization reference. It does not establish an absolute
per-cell increase, a causal molecular mechanism, or practical biological
importance. Those claims require design information and additional measurements.

# Common Misinterpretations

- **"Normalization removes biological differences."** A suitable method removes
  a nuisance scale while preserving feature-specific contrasts; a poor reference
  can erase real global biology or create artificial changes.
- **"The method with the flattest boxplots is best."** Identical marginal
  distributions are not a scientific requirement and can conceal genuine shifts.
- **"A factor is measured sequencing depth."** It is an estimated effective scale
  combining depth with a composition reference assumption.
- **"Spike-ins are an assumption-free gold standard."** Their calibration target,
  addition protocol, recovery, and sampling variability all matter.
- **"Normalization uncertainty is always negligible."** It may be consequential
  for small panels, pervasive shifts, sparse data, or factors driven by few genes.

1. RNA-seq counts identify relative composition, not total RNA abundance, without
   an external reference.
2. Composition bias occurs because changing one abundant component changes the
   denominator and therefore the apparent abundance of other components.
3. TMM and median-of-ratios use robust gene-wise consensus to estimate an
   effective sample scale.
4. Their validity depends on a sufficiently stable or balanced reference set;
   global asymmetric changes require external or prespecified controls.
5. Normalization factors solve neither batch confounding nor pseudoreplication,
   and their assumptions belong in the biological interpretation.
